architectural_implications.after: Generation, heuristic critique, and deterministic evidence collection are separate roles, with the main thread only synthesizing.

architectural_implications.observation: Evaluation is split out of the producing agent into independent blind sub-agents with distinct, non-overlapping evaluation criteria.

architectural_implications.before: Rules live as long prose ban-lists inside the prompt.
architectural_implications.consequence: Rules become non-compressible and consistently applied, but every new rule adds harness code to maintain and can conflict with model autonomy.
architectural_implications.observation: Constraint enforcement is moved below the prompt layer into deterministic hooks at the artifact boundary.

architectural_implications.after: Capability differences (e.g. sub-agent permissions) are designed for up front, with explicit stop-and-ask paths.
architectural_implications.before: A skill is tuned and assumed to work against the strongest available model/harness.
architectural_implications.consequence: Skill engineering becomes a compatibility/matrix problem, trading peak capability on strong models for uniform behavior across a heterogeneous fleet.
architectural_implications.observation: Skills are authored as portable artifacts compiled to multiple harnesses and validated against the weakest model in the fleet.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Paul Bakaus
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Skill engineering and building advanced harness systems for LLMs
  • Purpose: To share practical knowledge, design patterns, and lessons learned on scaling AI agent skills beyond simple prompting into robust harness engineering. Paul Bakaus presents 'The Dark Arts of Skill Engineering', exploring lessons learned from building 'Impeccable', a large enterprise application and skill. He contrasts basic prompting with 'harness engineering', detailing nine dark arts techniques such as blind sub-agent critiques, divergence enforcement, model routing, memory, interactive loops, compiler harnesses, and designing for the weakest model.

Topic Map

Introduction to Impeccable and Skill Engineering

  • Explanation: Introduction of Paul Bakaus and the Impeccable project, establishing the shift from prompt engineering to harness engineering.
  • Key claims:
    • Prompting is just the starter level; harness engineering is where you should end up.
    • Skills are an extension to coding harnesses.
  • Examples:
    • Building a kids reader iPad app using Claude code and frontend-design skill.
  • Terminology:
    • Impeccable
    • Skill engineering
    • Harness engineering
    • Frontend-design skill
    • Claude Code
  • Why it matters: Establishes the core philosophy that prompts alone are insufficient for complex, production-grade AI engineering.

The 9 Dark Arts of Skill Engineering

  • Explanation: Detailed breakdown of nine specific techniques and design patterns developed while building Impeccable.
  • Key claims:
    • Make them argue using blind sub-agents.
    • Force divergence instead of convergence.
    • Route in like a model.
    • Give them memory.
    • The script talks back.
    • Hooks that fight back.
    • Live wire the browser.
    • Compile to every harness.
    • Design for the weakest model.
  • Examples:
    • Using dual blind sub-agents for design critique to avoid anchoring bias.
    • Using anti-attractor seeds to force LLMs out of default aesthetic clusters.
  • Terminology:
    • Adversarial prompting
    • Anti-attractor
    • Sub-agents
    • Design linter
    • Prompt caching
    • Write-gate
  • Why it matters: Provides concrete architectural patterns for overcoming LLM biases, instruction following limits, and consistency issues.

Key Points

Prompting < Harness Engineering

  • Explanation: Simple prompts result in generic outputs (e.g., purple gradients, Inter font), whereas harness engineering structures constraints and agent behaviors.
  • Evidence: Analyzing the limitations of 55 lines of named bans in frontend-design prompts.
  • Practical implication: Engineers should wrap prompts in programmatic harnesses, linters, and multi-agent loops.

The Median is the Model's Gravity

  • Explanation: No amount of artisan prompt prose can overcome a model's latent space biases towards common choices.
  • Evidence: Tailwind's default theme defaults and historical web design trends.
  • Practical implication: You must use architectural mechanisms like anti-attractors to force divergence.

Blind Sub-Agents for Critique

  • Explanation: Asking an LLM to review its own work results in high self-ratings; spawning two blind sub-agents produces balanced critiques.
  • Evidence: Comparison of single-model code review vs. decoupled design director and deterministic detector sub-agents.
  • Practical implication: Implement adversarial sub-agent workflows for code review, design audits, and security checks.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The Two Blind Sub-Agents Critique Pattern

  • How it works: Spawns two blind sub-agents (e.g. design director and deterministic detector) that evaluate work independently before the main thread synthesizes their findings.
  • Components:
    • Sub-agent A (Design Director: hierarchy, slop, heuristics)
    • Sub-agent B (Detector: browser evidence, deterministic)
    • Main thread synthesis
  • When to use: Code reviews, design reviews, security audits, and ranking outputs.

The Reactive Loop (Live Browser Integration)

  • How it works: A tiny server injects a picker into a dev page; dragging a knob sends server-side events back to the running agent thread.
  • Components:
    • Tiny server injecting picker
    • Node live-poll MJS
    • Server-side event listener
    • Agent auto-wake on exit
  • When to use: Visual tweaking, interactive debugging, and iterative refinement of UI elements.

Examples & Case Studies

Codex refused to spawn sub-agents when first prompted.

  • Illustrates: Different LLMs have different permission models and instruction-following boundaries.
  • Lesson: You must explicitly instruct models when to stop and ask the user if they lack sub-agent permissions.

Generating 100 shades with a random seed and ranking them via a sub-agent.

  • Illustrates: Forcing divergence in color palette generation to avoid repeating default choices.
  • Lesson: Use creative random seeds and ranking sub-agents to escape latent space gravity.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Stop relying on pure prose prompts for complex tasks.
    • Implement write-gate hooks to catch formatting and styling errors before files hit disk.
    • Use anti-attractor seeds to push LLM generation out of common clusters.
  • Strategic:
    • Treat skill engineering as an extension of coding harness design.
    • Design your skills for the weakest target model in your deployment fleet.
    • Build passive guardrails rather than relying on commands users forget to run.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How do different LLM providers handle sub-agent spawning permissions?
    • What are the latency tradeoffs of multi-agent critique loops?
    • How can prompt caching be optimized when running reactive live browser loops?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Codex has a different permission model than Claude Code regarding sub-agent spawning. (technical behavior)
  • Context.mjs can automatically self-update if a new version of Impeccable is available. (architectural feature)

Notable Quotes

"The median is the model's gravity." "Two blind opinions beat one confident guess." "Passive guardrails beat a command no one remembers to run."

Compressed Summary

  • Prompting is the starter level; harness engineering is required for production AI skills.
  • LLMs suffer from latent space gravity; use anti-attractor seeds to force divergence.
  • Two blind sub-agents reviewing work independently yield better critiques than self-review.
  • Live-wiring the browser via reactive loops enables visual steering.
  • Design for the weakest model in your fleet and implement strict non-compressible gates.
  • Keywords: skill engineering, harness engineering, sub-agents, anti-attractor, design linter, reactive loop
  • Core insight: Prompting is merely a starter level; building robust AI skills requires advanced harness engineering, multi-agent adversarial critiques, and passive guardrails.

- **Illustrates**: Forcing divergence in color palette generation to avoid repeating default choices.
- **Lesson**: Use creative random seeds and ranking sub-agents to escape latent space gravity.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Stop relying on pure prose prompts for complex tasks.
  - Implement write-gate hooks to catch formatting and styling errors before files hit disk.
  - Use anti-attractor seeds to push LLM generation out of common clusters.
- **Strategic**:
  - Treat skill engineering as an extension of coding harness design.
  - Design your skills for the weakest target model in your deployment fleet.
  - Build passive guardrails rather than relying on commands users forget to run.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How do different LLM providers handle sub-agent spawning permissions?
  - What are the latency tradeoffs of multi-agent critique loops?
  - How can prompt caching be optimized when running reactive live browser loops?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Codex has a different permission model than Claude Code regarding sub-agent spawning. (technical behavior)
- Context.mjs can automatically self-update if a new version of Impeccable is available. (architectural feature)
## Notable Quotes
> "The median is the model's gravity."
> "Two blind opinions beat one confident guess."
> "Passive guardrails beat a command no one remembers to run."
## Compressed Summary
- Prompting is the starter level; harness engineering is required for production AI skills.
- LLMs suffer from latent space gravity; use anti-attractor seeds to force divergence.
- Two blind sub-agents reviewing work independently yield better critiques than self-review.
- Live-wiring the browser via reactive loops enables visual steering.
- Design for the weakest model in your fleet and implement strict non-compressible gates.
- **Keywords**: skill engineering, harness engineering, sub-agents, anti-attractor, design linter, reactive loop
- **Core insight**: Prompting is merely a starter level; building robust AI skills requires advanced harness engineering, multi-agent adversarial critiques, and passive guardrails.
